item.title: Oil and gas drillers optimistic heading into 2027, but warn of labour shortages
item.description: Oil and gas service firms say improving market conditions and a more supportive political climate are expected to bolster Canadian drilling activity next year.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: CALGARY — Oil and gas service firms say improving market conditions and a more supportive political climate are expected to bolster Canadian drilling activity next year, but labour shortfalls could threaten that momentum. Industry advocacy group Enserva has released its annual state of the industry report, which calls for an increase in the number of wells drilled in 2027 versus this year. But it flags competition for workers as a major challenge at a time when artificial intelligence data centres and major infrastructure projects draw from the same talent pool. Bradley Fedora, president and CEO of Trican Well Service Ltd., says the prospect of “hyperinflation” in the cost of labour and materials is what scares him most. Thomas Alford, president of completion and production services at Precision Drilling, told reporters at the event that it can take up to eight years to train up a competent drill rig staffer, and the industry has been so unstable in recent years that it’s been hard for those workers to get that consistent job experience. Gurpreet Lail, Enserva’s president and CEO, says the sector needs to work hard to attract and keep talent as data centre developments offer big paycheques to tradespeople and perks that have until now been “unheard of.” --- Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

item.title: CrowdStrike snaps up Zscaler in US$44B deal as cyber threats mount
item.description: CrowdStrike said on Monday it would buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal that values the company at about US$43.9 billion, in one of the largest cybersecurity deals on record, deepening its push into ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: CrowdStrike will acquire Zscaler in a US$43.9 billion all-stock deal, the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, uniting two major players as advances in artificial intelligence fuel increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s protection for computers, servers and other devices with Zscaler’s technology for securing employees’ access to applications and data, creating a broader cybersecurity platform for corporate and government customers. Zscaler shares jumped more than 13 per cent in trading to US$220.52, but remained well below the deal’s implied value of US$260.41 per share. CrowdStrike shares fell nearly 12 per cent. The gap between Zscaler’s trading price and the value of the offer comes as investors weigh the prospects for regulatory scrutiny of a transaction that would combine two of the cybersecurity industry’s biggest players. “Antitrust scrutiny is certainly possible given the size of the transaction and the importance of both companies, but it would be premature to assume that regulators will necessarily try to block it,” said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group. “The key issue is likely to be how much overlap regulators see between the two businesses and whether customers would genuinely have fewer competitive alternatives as a result.” The acquisition comes amid consolidation in the cybersecurity industry, with companies seeking to build broader platforms offering multiple services as customers look to reduce the number of security vendors they use. For CrowdStrike, the deal also opens up cross-selling opportunities by giving it access to roughly 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not currently use its products. Zscaler’s customer base includes large companies such as Unilever and United Airlines. Demand for cybersecurity tools has grown as enterprises worldwide confront increasingly sophisticated attacks, with advances in AI making it easier to identify and exploit software vulnerabilities while also improving tools designed to detect and stop threats. Recent outages affecting airlines, banks and government agencies, along with high-profile vulnerabilities in widely used Java and PHP software, have further heightened concerns over the resilience of critical digital infrastructure. Key deal terms Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share they own, implying a premium of about 34 per cent to Zscaler’s last close and an equity value of about US$42.46 billion. CrowdStrike shareholders will own about 84 per cent of the combined company after the transaction closes, which is expected in the second half of 2027. George Kurtz, CrowdStrike’s CEO, will lead the combined company, while Zscaler chief executive Jay Chaudhry will stay on to run the Zscaler business and join CrowdStrike’s board. The companies will continue to operate separately until closing. The agreement carries a US$1.4 billion breakup fee payable by Zscaler if it walks away under certain circumstances, including to accept a rival offer. CrowdStrike said the deal would expand its addressable market by more than US$185 billion, strengthening its position across a broader range of cybersecurity products and services. The combined company is expected to start with more than US$10 billion in annual recurring revenue, including roughly US$3.9 billion from Zscaler. CrowdStrike expects the deal to generate about US$1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing. Qatalyst Partners, JPMorgan and BofA Securities are advising CrowdStrike on the transaction, while BDT & MSD Partners, Citigroup and Goldman Sachs are advising Zscaler. Solid quarters for both The deal was announced alongside strong quarterly results from both companies. CrowdStrike forecast fourth-quarter revenue of between US$1.638 billion and US$1.644 billion, above analysts’ average estimate of US$1.62 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. It expects adjusted profit of 36 cents per share, in line with estimates. Third-quarter revenue rose 28 per cent to US$1.58 billion, helped by a 29 per cent increase in subscription revenue. Analysts had expected total revenue of US$1.53 billion. Adjusted profit was 34 cents per share, above estimates of 31 cents. Zscaler, meanwhile, reported a 20 per cent rise in first-quarter revenue to US$949.3 million, beating estimates of US$938 million. Adjusted profit of US$1.23 per share also topped estimates of US$1.16. --- Reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by Anil D’Silva and Vijay Kishore

item.title: S&P 500 most oversold since 2025 tariff tantum: Larry Berman
item.description: When evaluating markets from a technical perspective, oversold conditions are somewhat easier to trade than identifying market tops.
item.content:encoded:
When a market gets tactically oversold, a counter trend rally is inevitable. We obviously are seeing that today with Jensen being reinstated at Nvidia and Korea, Taiwan and China intervening in markets to curb short selling. When evaluating markets from a technical perspective, oversold conditions are somewhat easier to trade than identifying market tops. The basis for this is the understanding that people do not get anxious when making money, but they do when losing money.

This is the basis of the Nobel Prize winning Loss Aversion Theory (Kahneman, Tversky 2002). Investors tend to dislike losses twice as much as they like the same dollar value of a gain. This behaviour explains the skew we tend to see in how fast markets decline versus rally. Tactical risk monitor Last week, most of our 12 tactical factors were statistically oversold. Several breadth measures, volatility measures, and sentiment measures. The only positives were generally seasonal patterns. This combination suggests the bounce can get to the area of the old lows. For most of the past six months, the S&P 500 found support around 7300 where the 200-day average is sitting. For this bounce to be the beginning of a new rally leg, we need to hold above the 200-day average for more than a few days. How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google For now, we think this is an oversold bounce. We probably need another quarter of earnings to convince investors this is not the peak artificial intelligence (AI) period that many were concerned about. S&P 500 We are bullish on AI for the long-term, but the magnitude of the volatility swings suggests that more time is needed to work off some of the froth that built up. The good news is that the equal weight S&P 500 was still up about 10 per cent on the year at Friday’s close, so it’s clearly not a broad based sell off that would be the case if investors were worried about a recession.
